opening.headline: Learn how to distinguish which needs are covered by Google ADK's agents, workflows, callbacks, plugins, evaluations, and deployments.
body: Because the agent framework talks about workflow, callbacks, plugins, and sessions all at once, it feels hard to know where to start. However, each component is responsible for different needs, so starting from the needs creates an order.

In this class, we'll look at how the ADK starts small and grows its agents, moving through workflow agents whose sequence is controlled by code, callbacks that intervene at designated points, plugins that apply globally, and evaluation and deployment options to ensure quality. Next, we will look at the standards for whether code or model determines the order, the distinction between session, state, and memory, and the scope of application of callbacks and plugins.
As of 2026-10: gemini-2.5-flash in the example is provided primarily for existing users. In a new project, check and replace the currently accessible model ID and run the example.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain ADK's agents, workflow agents, callbacks, plugins, and deployment configurations
The scope of application of callbacks and plugins can be distinguished.
The structure in which the code determines the order and the structure in which the model determines the order can be distinguished by the predictability of the steps and the cost of failure.
Can explain differences in the scope of sessions, state, and memory

screens.title: I want to apply the same rules to all calls from the agent.
screens.lead:
First, read the needs of teams building customer support apps. Read while thinking about whether the request is a single-source issue or a multi-source issue.

As of 2026-10: gemini-2.5-flash in the example is provided primarily for existing users. In a new project, check and replace the currently accessible model ID and run the example.

visual.alt: A scene where we are trying to individually apply the same rules to three agents and multiple tools.
labels: Where is the distribution? How about quality?

paragraphs: Our customer support app has three agents and several tools. “Log all model calls and block unauthorized tools,” the team asks. If you try to solve this request by modifying the code for each agent and tool, something will inevitably be missed.

There are other needs too. I want to make sure that the ordered steps and iterative improvement steps are done in code rather than left to the model. This is because once the model establishes an order, it sometimes skips steps or changes the order.

Questions remain after development is complete. You need to decide where and how to distribute it and how to check its quality. Since the agent behaves probabilistically, we cannot be confident that it has passed once.

When a framework talks about workflow, callbacks, plugins, and sessions all at once, it's hard to know where to start. There is only one question in this class. How to divide structure, intervention points, deployment, and quality assurance within one framework. Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) answers component by component.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Can I implement the rule "Log all model calls" and the rule "Put an amount limit only on the refund tool" in the same way?

screens.outro: Let me first think about whether you have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Think of similar scenes
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think in your head first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever had to change logs or maintenance code that was scattered in several places at once and missed it?
items.answer: If you copy the same rule in multiple places, it's easy to miss the rest when editing one. We need a structure to put the rules in one place and apply them to multiple calls. This class covers that structure as a plugin.

items.prompt: Have you ever felt like, "I want to intercept and check just before this call?"
items.answer: There are moments when you want to check or block input right before a model call or tool call. A callback is a device that allows you to execute your function at a specified point without modifying the framework code.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced a problem with a prototype that worked well but got stuck during the deployment stage?
items.answer: Even agents that run well locally encounter new problems such as authentication, expansion, and cost in a deployment environment. Comparing deployment options with their degree of control and operational burden can help you avoid getting stuck.

It shows how ADK solves the above needs by dividing them into components. Workflow agents handle ordering, callbacks handle intervention at fixed points, plugins handle global rules, and evaluation and deployment options handle quality and operations.

screens.outro: First, let's look at what kind of framework ADK is and how to develop it.

screens.title: ADK Overview: A Framework for Starting Small and Growing
screens.lead: Select the right arrow and follow the process of creating and growing an agent with ADK step by step.

steps.title: What is ADK?
steps.body: The Agent Development Kit (ADK) is an open source framework for creating, debugging, and deploying reliable AI agents. Supports Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, and Kotlin. Its unique feature is that it gathers tools covering the entire agent development process in one place. It is advantageous for the team to be able to use the same concepts similarly in other languages.

steps.title: minimum agent
steps.body: A minimal agent is defined by a name, a model, instructions, and a few tools. For example, an agent with the name researcher and the Google search tool is the smallest unit.

steps.title: Start with prompt and tool invocation
steps.body: Initially, you start with just a prompt and a tool call. Focus on visually seeing what your agents are doing and finding areas where they are failing. Determining whether the results of a tool call are different from expectations is the starting point for improvement.

steps.title: grow up
steps.body: As the need arises, it grows into multi-agent combination, graph-based workflow, performance evaluation, and enterprise service deployment. You don't need to use all the features from the beginning, just add as much as you need.

steps.title: Model and Context
steps.body: You can use almost any generative model, easily access Gemini, and connect other model providers or local models with adapters. It is designed to adapt to your needs while efficiently managing context.

screens.outro: Let's look at the first component that divides the structure: the workflow agent.

screens.title: Workflow Agent: Code sets the order
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn why you need workflow agents, what types there are, and how template workflows work.

tabs.label: Why do you split it?
tabs.body: A single large agent becomes difficult to develop, evaluate, and maintain. Splitting it into multiple agents and execution nodes improves predictability, reliability, and structure. This is because the longer the instructions, the more different parts change when you fix one part. For example, splitting classification, drafting, and critique into independent agents means that fixing one has less impact on the rest.

tabs.label: Workflow type
tabs.body: Graph-based workflows weave agents and deterministic nodes into a branchable graph. Dynamic workflows structure the flow with code logic. A collaborative workflow consists of a coordinator agent and subagents. A template workflow is a set framework of sequential, looped, and parallel workflows.

tabs.label: Template workflow
tabs.body: The execution of template workflows is deterministic because it is controlled by defined code rather than an AI model. Subagents within it can use models, but the order is determined by the code. Sequential templates run subagents in order. This property ensures that they always run in the same order on the same input, making testing and debugging easier.

tabs.label: parallel template
tabs.body: Parallel templates run independent subagents simultaneously. Conversation history or status is not automatically shared between branches. To pass results, each branch must store the results in session state with a different key (e.g., different `output_key` for each branch) and then explicitly pass them in, and have subsequent steps read that key. So they are not suitable for tasks that require intermediate results from each other.

tabs.label: loop template
tabs.body: Loop templates repeat a set number of times or up to an ending condition. It doesn't stop on its own, so you either have to give it a maximum number of iterations or have a subagent signal it to stop. Agent routing, which selects one of several agents at runtime, is a separate feature.

screens.outro: Next, let's look at the criteria for determining whether the code or the model determines the order.

screens.title: Does the code or the model decide the order?
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how the right structure and its cost vary depending on how predetermined the steps are.

data.controlLabel: The degree to which steps are predetermined and the cost of failure.

stops.body: Like sorting, drafting, and reviewing, these are tasks where the steps and sequence are known from the beginning and a mistake can be costly. In this case, a workflow agent such as a sequence or loop where the code determines the order is appropriate. They run in the same order on the same input, making testing and debugging easier and eliminating the risk of your model skipping steps. Cost is flexibility. It cannot respond to situations outside the set path. Anthropic calls this structure, which links models and tools with defined code paths, a workflow, distinguishing it from an agent.

stops.value: Only the big picture is set
stops.body: Although the framework such as classification, parallel investigation, and synthesis is known, the content within each step is a task that varies from situation to situation. A mixed configuration is appropriate, where the skeleton is fixed as a workflow agent and the sub-agents of each step are determined by the model. Subagents within a workflow agent can use models and take advantage of the fact that only the order is determined by code. Prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-worker, and evaluator-optimization introduced by Anthropic are examples of these frameworks.

For tasks where it is impossible to know in advance how many steps are needed, such as investigating open questions or modifying code, an autonomous structure in which the model plans and selects tools on its own is appropriate. In ADK, an example is a collaborative workflow where a coordinator agent distributes work to subagents. The cost is clear. As calls increase, delays increase, execution becomes unpredictable, and errors can accumulate from step to step. So iteration caps, guardrails, and testing in isolated environments are necessary. Anthropic also recommends starting with the simplest solution and adding complexity only when the results actually improve.

stops.value: The cost of failure is very high.
stops.body: If there is a step that is difficult to reverse, such as executing a refund or deleting data, it is safer to fix that step in code and approve and verify it, even if the rest is autonomous. The criterion for judgment is whether errors at this stage can be reversed after the fact. The structure in which the code determines the order can make it mandatory to go through these steps, and leaving it to the model leaves the possibility of skipping those steps or executing them at the wrong time.

screens.outro: Next, we will distinguish between session, state, and memory where data is exchanged within the workflow.

screens.title: Sessions, state, memory: what goes where
screens.lead: Read the table to distinguish where conversation history, data during conversations, and knowledge beyond conversations are stored in the ADK. Later, the callback description says that it reads and updates session state.

data.caption: Comparison of sessions, state, and memory in ADK
rows: It is an event record that records the messages and agent's actions in that conversation in chronological order.
SessionService creates sessions, retrieves them, appends events, and deletes them.
These are the keys and values that are only needed for that conversation. Examples include items in your shopping cart or preferences expressed in conversation.
Managed by SessionService along with the session, it reads and writes to the session's `state`.
It is a knowledge repository that can be retrieved and used from past conversations or external sources.
MemoryService receives, stores, and retrieves session information through queries.
Different branches within the same execution
Conversation history or status is not automatically shared between branches.
Each branch stores the result in a different state as `output_key` and passes it to the next step to read it.
data.notes: The key distinction is that state is a per-interaction unit and memory is a trans-interaction unit. In-memory implementations used during development lose data when the app is restarted, so for long-term storage, use database or cloud-based implementations. This distinction also explains the previous screen's explanation that parallel templates do not automatically share state. The state resides in one place, the session, but the designer must decide which branch writes to which key.

screens.outro: Now, let's look at the code for callbacks that interrupt at fixed points in execution.

screens.title: Callback: Interrupting at a fixed point in execution
screens.lead: Please read the code alternately with the explanation on the right. This is a callback that checks the amount limit before calling the refund tool and records the result after calling it.

notes.note: Before Tool callback. If the amount exceeds the limit, it returns a value, skips running the tool, and writes that value as the tool result. Returning `None` continues the original flow. If you omit the tool name from the condition check, the limit will be applied to other tools as well.

After Tool callback. After the tool runs, it logs the input and results. Returning `None` leaves the result you just came across untouched, and returning a value replaces the tool's results with that value.

If you connect a callback when creating an agent, the framework will call it at a certain point. There are three pairs of branches. Immediately before and after full agent processing, before and after the LLM request and response, and before and after tool execution. This callback is specific to this agent and does not apply to tool calls from other agents.

The purpose of callbacks is for observation and debugging logs, data changes and bypass steps, guardrails such as safety rules and input/output validation, and reading and updating session state. Observe, change, and control without having to modify the framework code.

screens.outro: Let's compare plugins that extend callbacks globally.

screens.title: Plugin: Callbacks globally
screens.lead: Select the “Callback” and “Plugin” buttons alternately to compare the different coverage of the two devices.

visual.alt: An illustration comparing the scope of a callback being applied to one agent and a plugin being applied to the entire runner.
labels: Callback: Only for these agents and tools
Plugin: Register once and apply to all agents, tools and LLM calls

states.label: callback
states.body: A callback is a rule that is attached to one agent, one tool, or a specific task. It is suitable for rules with a clear target, such as checking the refund limit seen earlier. Since you connect directly when creating an agent, you can find out where and what rules are attached just by looking at the agent's definition. Conversely, if you want to apply the same rule to all agents, you must connect it to each agent.

states.label: plugin
states.body: Plugins are custom code modules that run at different stages of the agent workflow. Extend `BasePlugin` and define a callback method. Once a plug-in is registered with the Runner, or `App` object in Python, it is applied globally to all agents, tools, and LLM calls managed by that Runner. Typical uses include logging and tracing, policy enforcement (blocking unauthorized tool execution), monitoring and metrics, response caching, and request and response modification. For global functionality, such as safety rules, plugins offer greater modularity and flexibility than callbacks. Other examples provided include retry on tool failure, context filters, global directives, and per-call signature verification.

screens.outro: Now let's look at evaluation and deployment options to ensure quality.

screens.title: Evaluation and Deployment Options
screens.lead: By selecting and expanding each item, you can see how to check the quality of the agent and deployment options.

items.title: Why agent evaluations are different
items.body: Agents operate probabilistically, so simply checking pass and fail is not enough. You need to evaluate not only the final response, but also the sequence of steps leading to the goal, or trajectory. Even if the same final answer is reached, it is inefficient if there are many unnecessary tool calls.

items.title: Two components of assessment
items.body: One is the evaluation of the trajectory and tool use, and the other is the evaluation of the final response. Trajectory evaluation compares expected and actual step lists to look for errors and inefficiencies.

items.title: Method 1: Test file
items.body: The `.test.json` file is a small file containing one session, and a session can have multiple turns. This is a fast-paced unit test. A turn has user input, an expected tool call trajectory, an expected intermediate response, and an expected final response.

items.title: Method 2: Evaluation Set
items.body: This method uses a larger evaluation set when there is a large amount of data. While test files are for quick verification of individual features, evaluation sets are for quality checking on a wide range of inputs.

items.title: Decide before evaluation
items.body: Before evaluating, define your definition of success, key tasks, and metrics to track. An assessment without standards leaves no way to interpret the results.

items.title: Deployment Options
items.body: Agent Runtime on Google Cloud is fully managed and automatically scales. Cloud Run is a container-based managed environment. Choose GKE when you need more control or have an open model. Additionally, it can be uploaded to container environments such as Docker and Podman.

screens.outro: Now that you've seen all the concepts, let's explain the examples.

screens.title: Explanation 1: Flow that intercepts before and after calling a tool with a callback
screens.lead: The instructor walks you through how callbacks are inserted into refund tool calls. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: We want to check the amount limit before the refund tool is called and log the results after it is called. This rule is specific to one refund tool. Since the target is clear, a callback is the simplest choice.

steps.title: 1. Determine tool invocation
steps.body: The agent decides to call the refund tool. The tool has not run yet. This is where the Before Tool callback comes in. The callback is called after the model selects a tool but before the tool is actually executed.

steps.title: 2. If it is within the limit
steps.body: The Before Tool callback is executed. If the amount is within the limit, it returns nothing and the tool runs as is. In this case, the callback just checks the value without touching the tool.

steps.title: 3. If you exceed the limit
steps.body: If the amount exceeds the limit, the callback returns an alternative result, for example "Approval Required". The original tool call is skipped. The agent receives this value as the result of the tool and decides its next action. Users are notified that approval is required.

steps.title: 4. After execution
steps.body: When a tool runs, an After Tool callback logs the results or formats the response. Returning None leaves the result as is, returning a value replaces the tool's result with that value. By writing both before and after points like this, you can control before execution and record after execution.

screens.outro: Next, we will summarize the criteria for determining whether to use a callback or a plugin based on the scope of application.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Callback or plugin, divided by scope of application
screens.lead: As you select each need, the appropriate device and reason will unfold. Try responding to the needs of the first scene one by one. It becomes easier to judge if you first count how many areas are covered in each item.

items.prompt: Request 1: Set an amount limit on only one refund tool.
items.answer: The callback (Before Tool) is correct. Because they are rules attached to specific tools and tasks. If there is only one target, the callback is simple and can be found directly in the agent's definition. If the same rules become necessary for other agents' refund tools, then consider moving them to a plugin.

items.prompt: Request 2: Refine the response format of only one agent.
items.answer: Callback (After Model) is correct. It is a rule specific to that agent. Since responses from other agents should not be touched, no global device is used. The narrower the scope of application, the smaller the side effects.

items.prompt: Requirement 3: Log all agent, tool, and model calls.
items.answer: It's a plugin. Register once with Runner and apply globally. Even if new agents are added, the same log is automatically left. This is the case with the request in the first scene.

items.prompt: Requirement 4: Prevent unauthorized users from using any tools.
items.answer: It's a plugin. Safety rules must not be omitted, so it is important to cover them throughout, and a plug-in with good modularity is appropriate. This is the second request from the first scene.

items.prompt: Request 5: Reduce repeated calls to the same questions.
items.answer: The plugin (response caching) is correct. Reduce costs and delays by globally skipping expensive calls. This is because it is a service-wide policy, not a per-call policy.

screens.outro: Lastly, we will continue from development to deployment in one line.

screens.title: Commentary 3: From development to distribution in one line
screens.lead: The instructor walks you through the process of taking a customer support agent from definition to deployment. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: definition
steps.body: Define your support agent with name, model, instructions, and tools. At first, we start with a minimal configuration and grow by looking at failure cases. This definition becomes the starting point for all subsequent steps.

steps.title: workflow
steps.body: Sorting is the first step in a sequential template, while drafting and critique are looped templates to order the code. The loop specifies the maximum number of iterations. The order is determined by the code, so classification is never skipped. This structure is not subject to the whims of the model.

steps.title: intervention
steps.body: Tool-specific rules, such as refund limits, are placed in callbacks, and logs, permissions, and caching are globally registered in Runner as plugins. If you divide it by scope of application, nothing is left out. The two devices work together and do not replace each other.

steps.title: evaluation
steps.body: A test file compares the expected tool trajectory and final response with reality, and is rerun whenever changes are made. Before evaluating, define what success is and what metrics you want to track. If the evaluation results get worse, check at what stage the trajectory was off and correct that location.

steps.title: distribution
steps.body: Choose Agent Runtime if you need a managed runtime, Cloud Run if it's container-based, or GKE if you need more control. The choice is a balance between degree of control and operational burden. We continue to review evaluations after deployment to ensure quality is maintained. If this is your first deployment, starting with the fully managed option will have less operational overhead.

screens.outro: Now let's clean up the component map.

screens.title: Revisit the component map
screens.lead: The following flashcards describe the major components of the ADK. When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card. After checking all cards, proceed to the next screen.

cards.back: It is an open source framework that starts small and grows with multi-agent, graph, evaluation, and distribution. Name, model, instructions and tools are the minimum configuration. Example: An agent with the name researcher and the Google search tool. Almost any generative model can be connected.

Sequential, parallel, and loop templates are deterministically controlled by the code, not the model. A loop must have an exit device. Example: Let classification be the first step in a sequential template. Since the order is determined by code, testing is easy.

Observe, change, and block at points before and after agents, models, and tools. Returning None continues the original flow. Example: Before Tool callback that sets an amount limit only on the refund tool. Returning a value replaces that step.

Bundle callbacks, register them once with Runner or App, and apply them globally. It is suitable for logging, policy enforcement, and caching. Example: Globally block unauthorized tool execution. It is a global device with good modularity.

Trajectories and final responses are evaluated together. For deployment, choose between Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, GKE, and container environments to a degree of control. Example: Compare expected tool trajectory with actual trajectory. Before evaluating, define success first.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the order in which to decide where to place the rules.

screens.title: Order for deciding where to place rules
screens.lead: Let's group the contents of this lesson into a decision order that determines the location of the rule. Read it slowly.

paragraphs: When you want to impose a rule on an agent, the first question to ask is "Where does this rule apply?" If it only applies to one tool or agent, a callback is sufficient. If applicable for all calls, register once with Runner as a plugin.

The second question is, “Can we leave the order of these steps to the model?” If it must run in a certain order and a certain number of times, let the code control it with sequential, parallel, or loop templates. When writing a loop, you specify the maximum number of repetitions or a termination signal. Also keep in mind that state is not automatically shared between branches. If the answer to this question is “the model can decide,” a structure determined by the model, such as a collaborative workflow, is also an option.

The third question is “What determines quality?” Don't just look at the final response; also evaluate the trajectory of tool use. Before evaluating, you must define success and determine the metrics you will track before you can interpret the results.

The last question is distribution. Choose a managed runtime if you want to reduce operational burden, Cloud Run or a container environment if you want to handle containers directly, or GKE if you need more control.
These four questions can serve as a verbatim checklist in a design review meeting for a new agent project. Re-evaluate whenever changes are made to ensure the rule is behaving as intended.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The difference between callbacks and plugins is not their functionality but their scope of application. First decide whether you want to put the same rules in one place or everywhere.

glossary.def: They are sequential, parallel, loop templates where the defined code, not the model, determines the execution order of subagents.
This is a function I created that the framework calls at designated points in the agent, model, and tool.
A bundle of callbacks that you register once with Runner and apply to all agent, tool, and LLM calls.
A list of steps the agent goes through before responding to the user.
A fully managed, auto-scaling runtime for agents on Google Cloud.
A session is a record of the events of a single conversation, state is the keys and values within that session, and memory is a repository for retrieval across multiple sessions.

misconceptions.myth: Workflow agents are ordered by LLM.
misconceptions.fact: In template workflows, defined code deterministically controls the execution order of subagents. Subagents within it can use models, but the order is determined by the code.

misconceptions.myth: Callbacks and plugins are the same thing.
misconceptions.fact: Callbacks attach to one agent or tool, while plugins apply to the entire runner. Even though the function is the same, the scope of application is different.

misconceptions.myth: For evaluation, you only need to look at the final response.
misconceptions.fact: Trajectory evaluations that look at the sequence of steps and tool use should also be included. There may be inefficient paths to the same final answer.

misconceptions.myth: Agents running in parallel automatically see each other's results.
misconceptions.fact: Conversation history or status is not automatically shared between branches. We need to store the results in a state with different keys and explicitly pass them on for later steps to read.

closing.lead: The key contents of this class are summarized as follows.
points: ADK is an open source framework for defining and incrementally growing agents with names, models, instructions, and tools.
For sequential, parallel, and loop workflow agents, the code, not the model, determines the execution order.
Callbacks are attached to the forward and backward points of an agent, model, or tool and replace or continue the flow with a return value.
Plugins register once with the Runner and apply to all calls, so they fit global rules and safeguards.
For evaluation, look at both the trajectory and final response, and for deployment, choose between Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, GKE, and containers to a degree of control.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for you to think about for yourself. We will not submit or grade your answers, so feel free to think about them.
closing.reflection: Think of a rule you would like to place on your agent. Does that rule apply to just one tool or to all calls?
